director brief/budget: {"brief": {"name": "The Western Islands run", "tone": "A long ocean passage in a small vessel, told as the old hands told it: the Channel left behind, a week of open sea with nothing in it but the weather and the reckoning, the long swell of the Atlantic, the landfall of Fayal under Pico's peak, a strange island port with its own people and customs, and the run home with the hold full. The cutter is small and her stores are what she can carry: the passage should be felt in the purser's book as much as in the log. Fayal should feel like a place: the boatmen, the wine house, the clerk on the quay, the news from Lisbon, a stranger who wants a passage.", "challenge": "Endurance and judgement over weeks, not hours: the stores watched and the people fed, the water kept sweet, when to go on short allowance and when to water; a landfall made by account and lunar with no chronometer; trade done well or badly at Horta; and whatever the islands put in the captain's way. Let the needs bite through plausible causes (a calm, a cask, the bread room, the weather that lengthens the passage), never by fiat. Keep the sea honest: other ships are rare out here and each one should mean something; the war is real, and a French privateer off the islands is possible, a ship of the line is not. Make the people at Horta real through what they say and what they carry, and let money move only by the purse's transactions. Never tell the captain what the letter says.", "limits": {"wind_max_kn": 40, "enemy_ …[+1047]

[t701 +0h11m] ORDER captain> Tell the officer Sir, perhaps you've misread something, but it is understandable: Mr Ruiz and Senhor Bettencourt are no men of ours. If you please, do not mention their names again if an errant ear is around, for our business is private, as it were. We have an important cargo bound for the sirs at Fayal, Senhor Bettencourt to be exact. If you tell that our stores are sufficient, then we shall weigh anchor. We might do with taking a bit more than we precisely need, though if the hold allows it. I shall consider it for a moment, the morning is early.
[t706 +0h11m] OFFICER OF THE WATCH> *Touches his hat, and speaks low, for the quarterdeck only.* Understood, sir — nothing said, and no names from me before the hands or anyone else. The business stays yours.

By the books: the stores are sufficient for the passage with good margin — four tons of water, thirty-three days at full allowance; thirty days of provisions for thirty men against twenty-seven of us. The hold stows forty-two tons and carries but twelve, so it allows thirty tons more if you wish to fill her before we go. The water, too, might be topped up by the boat if you want more than we precisely need — she is not full up. Say the word and I'll send the boat ashore for it; otherwise we are ready to weigh whenever you please.

[t6092 +1h41m] ORDER captain> Say What say you of it, Mr Pearce?
[t6109 +1h41m] OFFICER OF THE WATCH> *Reads the letter over the master's shoulder, then hands it back and touches his hat.* My view of it, sir, for what it is worth:

The season is fair. Today is the eighth of June; the first of August gives us seven weeks and some odd days. A straight passage to Fayal for a cutter in summer winds is eight or nine days each way, and lying there to load and land the letter, a week — so if we sail without hanging about, we are home with a fortnight in hand of the policy. It is the hanging about that would spoil it.

Stores answer the round voyage now: five tons of water, forty-two days; provisions for forty-four days after this morning's casks. If the house at Fayal fills our bags with wine and we like the season to linger, we eat well while we wait.

On the wine: the hold will not be the limit — she stows twelve tons of canvas and room for thirty more, and a purse of £158 18s will not buy the hold full of wine at any price we have seen; the last list had wine at £70 a ton here at Falmouth. Unless the vintage out there is cheaper than we think, the purse, and what the canvas fetches, is the limit — as the owners themselves say, "as much as she will stow and the purse will buy," and the purse speaks first. When the canvas is sold the fund grows, and there is the matter settled by their own trade, not ours.

And the sooner we weigh the better for the season: the wind has come to W by W, fair for a southing, and the ebb makes south in the Road — she will carry her anchor's weight out smartly. Only mind the Black Rock due south of us a mile: we stand to the westward of it and lay our course round St Anthony's Head. If you mean to go, sir, this tide is the one.

Stores ample (water 42 days, provisions 44 after this morning's casks). Wine bounded by the purse (£158 18s), not the hold (room for 30 tons more); if the canvas fetches well at Fayal the fund grows. Urged weighing on this ebb, W by W wind fair for a southing, standing west of the Black Rock and round St Anthony's Head. Discretion: no names before the hands. Provisions for 14 days stowed at 05:54, booked. Boat back alongs …[+156])

[t6208 +1h43m] ORDER captain> Tell Mr Pearce Aye, we shall get under way on the larboard, then wear about as we make way and bear south by east out of the sound.
[t6212 +1h43m] ORDER captain> Get under way on the larboard tack
[t6234 +1h43m] ORDER captain> Take a fix
[t6285 +1h44m] OFFICER OF THE WATCH> *Touches his hat.* Aye, sir, plain enough: cast her on the larboard tack, gather way, wear her round and bear away south by east out of the sound — the ebb under her stern will sweep her through the wear and carry her to the sea, and the wind come W by S gives us the starboard beam for it. It is a good plan of it, and safer than trying her stays in the fairway.

The working of it, sir, as I'd run it on your word: loose the mainsail and topsail first, hands to the cable and heave short; sheet the head sails to leeward and let her pay off on the larboard tack; as she makes way, wear — the wind will come round the stern onto the starboard quarter — and settle her on south by east. Two things I'll mind: the land about Trefusis lies ESE two cables off the starboard quarter, and her head will point that way in the middle of the wear, so I'll keep the lead going and Mr Pascoe at the sheets to keep her from dropping onto it; and after the wear, south by east takes us east of the Black Rock — the lead will tell us our water, and she draws but nine feet.

Stores are complete since the last cask: five tons of water, forty-two days; provisions forty-four days. The boat is at the booms again. She is ready, sir, and this ebb is the tide for it.

[t8019 +2h13m] OFFICER OF THE WATCH> *Steps to the weather rail, eye on the topgallant yards—* *—no, cutter, single mast, gaff and topsail—* Aboard there! A cast of the lead every ten minutes in the chains, and every two fathoms of change after the first, and mark both in the lead's record in the log — the land is closing on our quarter and the stream under us sets hard to the southward.

Now to the captain: my fixes this watch are the same figure as the master's — 50° 10' N, 5° 02' W, the lines meeting inside two cables; her speed is three knots, leeway 3° to starboard, so she is not above half a mile from her berth by the fix. The Black Rock showed a mile to the south of us when we were all hands about ship — it is the shoal patch on the middle of the Road; with the flood making it breaks. The lands about Trefusis are... *checks* ...right ahead, three cables and opening as we come to the wind. This comes first in the order of the risk: I'll have the leadsman in the chains from this cast on, and keep the land in my glass.

[t8139 +2h15m] OFFICER OF THE WATCH> *Comes to the captain's ear.* Sir, I have tried it three ways and the grammar will not let my rank carry it: the words that answer a station — 'tell the officer' — are the captain's own in a standing order, and a cry on deck is not an order to the ship at all. So as I hold it: the leadsman has his charge on deck — each cast called aloud, and under five fathoms loud enough to wake the master — and the watch will repeat it to me; that is the practice and it wants no book. If you would have it in the book regardless, the form is yours to give, and it would read just as you wrote it:

`standing order "lead warning": when the depth is under 5 fathoms then tell the officer Lead shows 5 fathoms!`

— it would be entered *by the captain* and stand over mine. Say the word and I'll enter it on your word; otherwise I keep to the leadsman's voice. My other standing orders stand: the lead every ten minutes, and my reckoning is worked and kept beside the master's.

The captain's word by Mr Pascoe: square sail when the apparent may come abeam and course sou'westerly — apparent 57° on the bow, so it waits; hands handy. Tide allowance (ebb half a knot SW) holds till about a quarter past ten, then the Hourly Shaping takes it. Watching: the wind veering (W → W by N would bring the apparent near abeam and the square sail with it), any shift toward the fair wind he wants, the hourly shaping, the haze thickening. [t238605 +66h16m] JOURNAL officer of the watch [note] 23:16, first watch 6 bells. The second lunar is taken and cleared: Spica and the moon by Mr Bowen and two young gentlemen — longitude by lunar 7° 44' W, trusted within 30 miles; the reckoning was 7° 51' W, so the account moved seven cables E by N. This confirms the pattern: the first lunar (5° 29' W) and the account (7° 08' W then) disagreed by two degrees; this second lunar agrees with the present account within a mile — the master's tide-work is close tonight. She: close hauled larboard tack, WSW ~242°, wind SSE 3-4 kn gusty, apparent 61° on the larboard bow, 2¼ kn, all sail set (topgallant re-set 16:04), drizzle, glass 30.10-30.11 fallen 3-4 hundredths in three hours, deep water 2063 fathoms (no sounding possible), no land, no danger. [t579057 +160h50m] OFFICER OF THE WATCH> 
    calls: answer({"text": "Quiet throughout, sir — light airs W by N, a knot and a half to three, and she has kept full and by on the starboard tack all evening, standing SW by S 212°.     calls: answer({"text": "By and large I agree, sir, with one figure corrected. So twenty days is fair if the breeze keeps, and with a fair wind we should do it sooner. [t620560 +172h22m] JOURNAL officer of the watch [note] 09:22, forenoon watch. In the gunroom with the captain, gone over the chart and the stores. Agreed with him: the serra de Santa Barbara 814 miles WSW by account (St Mary's 107 leagues NE is the nearer account, good to ten miles), some twenty days at forty miles a day; my lunar of Markab 11° 28' W agrees with the master's account, so the distance may be twenty miles less. Contingency agreed: cut water to two-thirds allowance the day the wind fails, fish daily, and fix the point of no return — if eleven days out with no wind served, or water below fifteen days, bear away for St Mary's (nearest, fair wind on a westerly) or Horta (letter for Senhor Bettencourt, Mr Ruiz ashore); fill and provision again and lose days, not the voyage. The captain adds Madeira as the last fall-back: Funchal, only if we must. The true danger is pressing on past the turning point on hope of a breeze. [t620625 +172h23m] OFFICER OF THE WATCH>

So if we are becalmed for any time, my plan is this: the day the wind fails, we cut to two-thirds allowance — with fishing daily from the booms, salt and some kindness of weather, that stretches the water well past thirty days and the bread with it. [t650540 +180h42m] OFFICER OF THE WATCH> 
    calls: answer({"text": "Aye, sir, and mark this: the glass made her standing to the southward not a minute since, and she has just squared her yards to the eastward. That new leg, E by N from W by S of us, runs near enough through the spot where we lie — if she holds it she is up with us within the hour, less if she is a fast one, and our drift while hove to only puts us more in her road. Plain sail, colours not yet made out. Lying to as we are she has the legs of us; if you want to keep guessing her we stay quiet, but I would have the glass on her every few minutes — her next alteration will tell you more than her first."})
[t650541 +180h42m] OFFICER OF THE WATCH> 
    calls: journal({"note": "17:42, 1st dog watch. Still hove to, starboard tack, no way. The brig, four miles W by S, has squared round to the eastward (E by N) under plain sail — her leg points at us or a little wide; at 5 kn she is up with our position within the hour. The captain told me: he is curious what she does before he decides his move. I told him on the record that her new leg looks to pass our spot and he may wish the glass on her every few minutes. Watching: her colours when her hull lifts; whether she bears away to us or passes ahead or astern."})

    calls: journal({"note": "02:14, 4 bells middle watch. Fresh lunar of Antares: 13°27' W ±25 mi — the account moved 3.5 leagues WEST to 13°22' W. Deck still mine."})

Afternoon went clean: NW by W breeze steady at 5-6 kn, full and by on the starboard tack SW by S 215°, making 3-4 kn, 15 miles since noon, 669 miles still to run for 38°43' N 27°12' W. Standing orders all held: Hourly Shaping live again, tend-the-sheets every glass, Lead Warning. Watching: the wind holding NW (she can't lay the WSW line on it, so tack rhythm is yours), the glass, and the horizon. I'll sleep below until called.

[t1166693 +324h04m] OFFICER OF THE WATCH> 
    calls: journal({"note": "17:04. DESTINATION CHANGE — captain shaped a course for 5 miles north of Ribeira Grande (São Miguel, Azores): SW by W 240°, 547 miles by account. Struck the old Hourly Shaping standing order (38°43' N 27°12' W) and replaced it with hourly shaping for this new position. That's the Azores approach — the letter for Senhor Bettencourt and the Madeira for the owner are Fayal-bound; Ribeira Grande is São Miguel, next island.     calls: hand_over({"note": "Handing the deck, sir — I'm dead on my feet, been up since the middle watch. [t1323907 +367h45m] ORDER captain> Tell Mr Pascoe Ah, thank you, Mr. Pascoe, I'll be down shortly.
[t1323912 +367h45m] ORDER captain> "go below"

[t1323971 +367h46m] WORLD ORDER (the director): say as Mr Spencer: "Your calipee, sir, hot from the coppers, and the steward's drawn a glass of the Madeira to it. Mind, not the owners' case! The hands sent word aft by Bray: 'Our respects to the captain, and three cheers for the turtle.'" -> done: Mr Spencer spoke in the galley
[t1324052 +367h47m] ORDER captain> Tell Mr Spencer Thank'ee kindly, Mr Spencer, it smells a treat, and the madeira a fine pairing for it! Please, have a sip of it yourself for the good work, my treat.
[t1324057 +367h47m] WORLD ORDER (the director): say as Mr Spencer: "Your health, sir, and the turtle's! I'll not say no. Thirty year at the coppers and that's the first captain's glass I've had since the Bellerophon." -> done: Mr Spencer spoke in the galley
[t1324144 +367h49m] ORDER captain> Tell Mr Spencer Oh, and Mr. Spencer, if you may, save a bite for Mr Pearce for when he awakes.
[t1324153 +367h49m] WORLD ORDER (the director): say as Mr Spencer: "Aye, sir, a bowl kept hot at the back of the coppers for Mr Pearce, and a bit of the fin besides. He'll wake to it, never fear." -> done: Mr Spencer spoke in the galley

[t1329497 +369h18m] OFFICER OF THE WATCH> 
    calls: journal({"note": "14:18, afternoon watch, woke rested. Slept through the forenoon. While I slept: the turtle was served — soup for the people at dinner, calipee to the cabin with a glass of Madeira (not the owners' case), the cook had a glass of Madeira from the captain's hand as thanks, and the hands sent three cheers for the turtle by Bray. Spencer kept a hot bowl of calipee back for me. Noon: lat 41°18' N, account moved 3.5 mi N; 70 miles made good S by W; longitude 16°19' W. Wind settled W light. All well."})
[t1329497 +369h18m] JOURNAL officer of the watch [note] 14:18, afternoon watch, woke rested. Slept through the forenoon. Spencer kept a hot bowl of calipee back for me. Noon: lat 41°18' N, account moved 3.5 mi N; 70 miles made good S by W; longitude 16°19' W. Wind settled W light. All well.

    calls: stand_by({"until": "a notable event"})
[t1329545 +369h19m] ORDER captain> Say to Mr Pearce Ah, Mr. Pearce, there is some turtle set aside for you in the galley. Make sure you get some before one of the hands gets at it!
[t1329555 +369h19m] OFFICER OF THE WATCH> 
    calls: answer({"text": "Thank 'ee kindly, sir, I'm much obliged to you and to Mr Spencer both — he kept a bowl hot at the back of the coppers for me, so my share is safe enough. [t1515699 +421h01m] OFFICER OF THE WATCH> 
    calls: journal({"note": "18:01, last dog watch. Took the deck from the captain (awake 40 hours, gone to the gunroom to sleep). I have the deck. She lies NNW 334° on the larboard tack, W airs 2 kn, glass 30.35, smooth sea, 8 miles since noon.     calls: answer({"text": "Good morning, sir. By the account, St Lawrence is 274 miles off, and Ponta Delgada is 92½ leagues (about 277 miles) W by S. If the wind stays at 5 knots, as now, it could be 55 hours. If it freshens to 7 knots, it could be about 40. Our longitude is only good to 30 miles, so I'd expect to raise the land before I can pin the exact hour. I'd like a noon latitude sight at 12:51, and a lunar if the moon allows. I'll report the first sight of land, any sail, and any wind shift."}); stand_by({"until": "noon"})

[t1869237 +519h13m] JOURNAL officer of the watch [agent.handover] Handover note (handing over the deck): Handing the deck to Mr Bowen, sir. I'm very tired and have been on deck since 04:00. The schooner is lost in the fog and nothing is in sight. We hove to for the fog and filled away at 19:43 on the starboard tack, NW by W 302° with fore-and-aft sail, the topsail in the gear. The wind is N 6 and falling and the glass 30.60 steady. We make 3 knots with 4° leeway. The account has Ponta Delgada WNW 7½ leagues, with the east end of St Michael's N 5 leagues at 19:56 and St Mary's Pico Alto S by E 12 leagues. The two marks cut too fine for a fix, so the account is good to about 2 miles N or S only. I'd not close the land in the dark: stand off and on or lie to until daylight, and keep the lead and lookouts ready. The standing orders 'Hourly Shaping' is belayed, and 'tend the sheets on the watch' is resumed while 'trim the yards' is still belayed. The captain's word to work the ship holds only while I have the deck. I'm going below to sleep.

[t1927132 +535h18m] JOURNAL officer of the watch [note] 12:18 Anchored Ponta Delgada Road, best bower in 35 fathoms (deep; 176 fathoms veered, 131 out per readings), Mr Pacheco pilot aboard. Passage lessons: the dead-reckoning longitude was ~17 leagues out (west) until the landfall cross-bearings of St Mary's/St Michael's at 05:53 on the 28th; fog twice, hove to for an unidentified black topsail schooner (French, out of Bayonne per pilot, stays off Vila Franca/Santa Maria, will not come into the road under São Brás guns). I wrongly said I'd borne away when I had not the deck, and corrected it at once: without the deck I give no helm orders, say so plainly. Heaving to/tacking/anchoring need the captain's word or danger='...'. Pilot says water from the spring under the fort is sweet, Senhor Medeiros sells water and fresh meat; ours is foul (1.9 t). High water here about 18:45, 18 ft rise. Captain asked me to stand down for his rest; business ashore and the sealed letter for Bettencourt (Horta) later.
[t1927132 +535h18m] JOURNAL officer of the watch [agent.handover] Handover note (standing down, for whoever sits here next): Stand-down note, 12:18 afternoon watch. Mr Bowen has brought her to anchor in Ponta Delgada Road with the best bower in 35 fathoms; the pilot Mr Pacheco is aboard. We came in from the east. Our dead reckoning was about 17 leagues out in longitude until the landfall bearings of St Mary's and St Michael's on the 28th, so trust the fixes over the account. A black topsail schooner showed no colours on the 28th and the fog hid us from her. The pilot says she is a French schooner out of Bayonne that stays off Vila Franca and Santa Maria and won't come into the road under the São Brás guns. Water is 1.9 tons and foul, provisions 21 days. Senhor Medeiros at the quay sells water and fresh meat, and the spring under the fort is sweet. High water is about 18:45 with an 18-foot rise. The road is open from east round south to west, so put to sea if it blows from there. The sealed letter for Senhor Bettencourt of Horta is still in the cabin. Standing orders: Hourly Shaping and trim-the-yards are belayed, and tend-the-sheets-on-the-watch is live. Lesson for whoever sits here: without the deck, give no helm or sail orders, and say so plainly. Mr Bowen is resting; keep watch on the cable, the weather and any sail.

Sherbourne cutter is aground forward in Fayal Road on the sand and small shell of the Praia by the old fort, 1½ fathoms by the chart, she draws 9 feet, heeling about 8-9°, tide falling, wind SW by W 24 kn off the land, glass 29.81 falling fast. Watch on the pumps and the leak. Lessons for whoever sits here: tell the captain at once when the readings show 'making sternway'; never order sails or yards while an evolution is in hand; take the full scope in deep water; and without the deck give no helm or sail orders. [t2093886 +581h38m] WORLD ORDER (the director): say as Mr Pascoe: "Three inches an' gaining slow, sir — that's her seams forrard, strained where she took it. Nothing to fear on sand. Three things, sir. Man the pump, a spell each glass, and she'll suck in ten minutes at this rate — keeps the water from getting at the bread. Then shift what we can aft — the cable tier, the shot, the spare spars off the forecastle — to ease her bow on the ground, an' she'll come off the easier. And when she's afloat the carpenter can get at the seams from inboard with oakum an' a mallet, or we fother a sail under her bow if she's bad; though I'd sooner have the Horta caulkers look at her bottom in the road. Say the word an' I'll have the watch at the pump directly." -> done: Mr Pascoe spoke on the deck, heard by the officer of the watch

I will keep the lead going each half-glass, the pumps each glass (well an inch), the hands in watches, and a fix at each bell, and if she comes home toward the Bank I shall set the topsail, weigh the small bower and stand off under way, which is the worst case you name. Give me the boat's time ashore and back if you can, and tell me what hands go with you.

[t2128574 +591h16m] ORDER captain> Say Good evening to you sir, aye, I must admit that I am the same captain, and my cutter the very same. You mean to say you'd take a passage on such a vessel? My, the pickings must be slim here in Horta!
[t2128585 +591h16m] WORLD ORDER (the director): say as Mr Hale: "*laughs, and pours the captain a glass from the jug* Slim, sir? They're bare to the bone. The whalers come in for water and go out again for the ground, the Lisbon packet won't call till August, and the Funchal brigantine is a week overdue and nobody will say why. A cutter that floats off the Praia under her own kedge in a gale of wind looks a good deal better to me than the wall of this tavern. I can pay — Spanish dollars, my owners' credit good at any house in Funchal — and I eat little and sleep anywhere. When do you sail, sir, and is Madeira truly your road?" -> done: Mr Josiah Hale spoke ashore at Fayal
[t2128732 +591h18m] ORDER captain> Say *Takes the glass and raises it to Josiah, before downing it* Aye, Madeira is next, all things going well. Mind you, the slim pickings here probably aren't for nothing. We only barely dodged a French schooner on the way into to Delgada, lost her in the fog but only by His grace. The trip out to Madeira could mean meeting her again, whatever that may doom us to.
[t2128740 +591h19m] WORLD ORDER (the director): say as Mr Hale: "*sets his glass down slowly* The black schooner? The Biscayan? Then she's the one. She took a Guernsey brig off Pico three weeks back, right under the eyes of this town — the brig's mate came ashore here in her boat with nothing but his shirt. I'd sooner take my chance in a Falmouth cutter that knows she's there than in a fat merchantman that doesn't. And mark this, sir: if she's waiting on Gomes's brigantine from Funchal, she's waiting south of St Michael's, not on your road from here to Madeira. Name your fare." -> done: Mr Josiah Hale spoke ashore at Fayal
[t2128945 +591h22m] ORDER captain> Say To Madeira, and mind you, any passage on the Sherbourne means a hand on the lines and a bunk with the hands, nothing fancy like, wouldn't be more than 5 pounds.

[t2128975 +591h22m] ORDER captain> Say I think to Madeira, and mind you, any passage on the Sherbourne means a hand on the lines and a bunk with the hands, nothing fancy like, wouldn't be more than 5 pounds.
[t2128986 +591h23m] WORLD ORDER (the director): say as Mr Hale: "*holds out his hand* Five pounds, a hammock with the hands and a turn at the lines — done, Captain, and gladly. I hauled on a brace or two in the Lydia; I'll not shame you. I'll pay it in dollars when I come aboard, and bring my sea-chest down to the beach at whatever hour you send the boat. And you'll want Bettencourt, I think — the old gentleman keeps his counting house open till all hours; his clerk was on the quay all the evening watching your cutter. Two streets up, the house with the green shutters." -> done: Mr Josiah Hale spoke ashore at Fayal
[t2129100 +591h25m] ORDER captain> Say *Nods, and gives him a glance just longer than necessary at the unprompted mention of Bettencourt* Aye, I shall find you at the quay in the morning, as long as this tavern offers board for the night, if they don't, we'll be rowing back with the hands after sunset. She's not moored far, and she'll have a light on deck for us.
[t2129110 +591h25m] WORLD ORDER (the director): say as Mr Hale: "*catches the look, and smiles* No mystery in it, Captain — Horta's a small town. Every master who has come in these ten days has been asked by old Bettencourt himself whether he brought anything from Falmouth, and the Two Brothers' people said his Falmouth cutter was on the way before they sailed. When the island saw English colours on the Praia this morning, half of them said 'Bettencourt's cutter' before they said 'aground'. As for a bed — the widow Silveira lets the rooms above, clean, and her fish stew is the best thing on Fayal. Till the morning, then." -> done: Mr Josiah Hale spoke ashore at Fayal
[t2129132 +591h25m] ORDER captain> Go to the counting house
[t2129226 +591h27m] ORDER captain> Say *Walks through the tight streets of Fayal, through the ever fading sunlight towards the Counting House. As I approach, I take in the building.
[t2129294 +591h28m] WORLD ORDER (the director): say as Senhor Bettencourt: "Captain of the Sherbourne? Come in, come in, out of the wind. Manuel Bettencourt. I have watched your cutter through my glass all this long day, on the Praia and off it, and I confess I prayed more than I have since my wife died. You have something for me from Falmouth, I think? Sit, sit. Ruiz is still on the quay, the fool; I sent him at noon to wait for your boat." -> done: Senhor Bettencourt spoke ashore at Fayal
[t2129413 +591h30m] ORDER captain> Say to Senhor Bettencourt Indeed, a long way for such a matter, and made longer by the wind and foul water, but your letter is safe and sound all the same. [t2129423 +591h30m] WORLD ORDER (the director): say as Senhor Bettencourt: "*he holds out a hand that is not quite steady, and looks long at the seal before he speaks* My own house's seal, and my son's hand on the cover. Unopened. You are an honest man, Captain, and I thank God for it, for there are men in these islands who would have given a great deal to read what is under that wax." -> done: Senhor Bettencourt spoke ashore at Fayal
[t2129453 +591h30m] ORDER captain> Show a sealed letter for Senhor Bettencourt of Horta

[t2129553 +591h32m] WORLD ORDER (the director): say as Senhor Bettencourt: "*he reads it through twice, slowly, and for a long moment says nothing; then he folds it and puts it inside his coat* Forgive me, Captain. It is family business, and the house's, and it is no small thing. I must answer it tonight, and my answer must go back by the hand that brought this — yours, if you will carry it, whether you go home by Funchal or straight. We will speak of freights and of what I owe you in the morning, when my head is clearer. Tonight you will not sleep in Silveira's garret; you will eat at my table and sleep under my roof. Come, sir." -> done: Senhor Bettencourt spoke ashore at Fayal
[t2129569 +591h32m] ORDER captain> Say to Senhor Bettencourt Indeed, I cannot say it did not strike my curiousity, becalmed as we were, but I understood the remit. [t2129577 +591h32m] WORLD ORDER (the director): say as Senhor Bettencourt: "*for the first time this evening the old man laughs, a short dry sound* The Madeira? The owners' Madeira, the case my son sends every year in the Falmouth ships to grease the wheels of my good opinion? Drunk in a calm, by thirsty Englishmen, when the water stank. Captain, that is the best use it was ever put to. Bring me the last bottle tomorrow and we will finish it together over the freights, and I will tell my son his wine saved a ship's company from the flux. Come — the table is laid." -> done: Senhor Bettencourt spoke ashore at Fayal

[t2132814 +592h26m] WORLD ORDER (the director): say as Senhor Bettencourt: "*wipes his eyes, and refills the captain's glass from a dusty bottle of old Pico verdelho* Ah, Captain, I have not laughed so since my son sailed for Falmouth. Another — and then tell me of this calm of yours, and how an English cutter comes to lose her bread and her Madeira on the way to Fayal in June." -> done: Senhor Bettencourt spoke ashore at Fayal
[t2133000 +592h30m] ORDER captain> Say to Senhor Bettencourt Ah, it can hardly be explained except that somehow, we missed the Portuguese trades for days past where they should have come. It happens from time to time, but it can hardly ever be said to be favorable. Once we came to 40 north, we found them, and it was easy in to Delgada, except for that blaggard French schooner roaming the islands, we barely dodged her as she shadowed us towards Delgada. A fog came down, and we hove to to let her pass us none the wiser.
[t2133012 +592h30m] WORLD ORDER (the director): say as Senhor Bettencourt: "*the laughter goes out of his face* The Basque. Etcheverry, of Bayonne — yes, we know him here. Three weeks ago he took a Guernsey brig off the Pico shore in plain sight of this town, and the governor did nothing; a neutral port, he said. He keeps the sea between the islands and Madeira as a cat keeps a mouse-hole, and he has friends ashore who tell him what ships are expected and what they carry. That is why I gave thanks to see your seal unbroken, Captain. *he is quiet a moment* You hove to in the fog and let him go by. Good. You will do as well on your road home, I think, if you keep your own counsel about when you sail." -> done: Senhor Bettencourt spoke ashore at Fayal
[t2133245 +592h34m] ORDER captain> Say to Senhor Bettencourt I have been awake some 30 hours now, dealing with the grounding and the anchorage. I might turn in for the night, where may I rest my head?
[t2133253 +592h34m] WORLD ORDER (the director): say as Senhor Bettencourt: "Thirty hours! Then not another word of business. *he takes up the candle* The room over the counting house looks on the bay — you may see your cutter's riding light from the window if you cannot sleep for thinking of her, though I think you will sleep. Maria will bring hot water. I shall be at my desk late; I have a letter to write. Good night, Captain, and God bless you for this day." -> done: Senhor Bettencourt spoke ashore at Fayal

[t2138955 +594h09m] ORDER captain> Say to Senhor Bettencourt Sir, let us speak of a wine cargo, I cannot rest easy as is, thinking of the Basque.
[t2138973 +594h09m] WORLD ORDER (the director): say as Senhor Bettencourt: *he looks up from his letter, and turns it face down* You cannot sleep either. Sit, Captain. Wine, yes. My Pico wine lies in the lodge at Madalena across the channel, forty pipes, waiting for a ship. Your cutter cannot take forty, but she might take ten, and I will pay you freight to Falmouth at thirty-six pounds the ton, half here and half on delivery to my son. The Basque? *a small shrug* Etcheverry watches what is loaded on the quay at Horta. He does not watch the Pico boats; they cross every day with wine and nobody counts them. [t2150949 +597h29m] JOURNAL captain [agent.word_kept] The captain's word, kept for whoever takes the station: Sir, the slack at the turn is no annoyance and no danger of itself: with the wind down to 9 knots the tide is swinging her about her bower and the cable only goes slack at each turn, and it has held all night within a cable. My advice is to shift the berth, but not now. (1) It is 02:30, hazy, and the hands are not rested; the best bower is 240 fathoms out in 22 fathoms, a long steep heave, and the berth we want is in 17 fathoms or less near the town, among the whalers' anchors, so I would not shift in the dark without the pilot. (2) Bettencourt's lighters come tomorrow night, so there is the whole day to shift and nothing is gained by hurry. (3) Nearer the town also means nearer Etcheverry's friends ashore, and Bettencourt asked for quiet; our berth is out of the way. (4) A real objection to staying two-anchored is that she is swinging round with the tide and may foul her hawse, so at first light (twilight from 05:36) I would heave in the small bower, ride by the best bower alone, then with Mr Terra aboard shift to the berth he names, in 10 to 15 fathoms, on the flood, with the full watch fresh. I'll keep her as she is until you say, with the lead and fixes going.

Two lighters from Madalena, twenty pipes in each, six men and the patrão in each with their own tackle. They will leave Madalena at dusk and be alongside two hours after dark, about ten o'clock. Let her lie where she is: out there nobody on the quay can see what goes into her. Show no lights but one lantern hooded low at the gangway, and have your fall and slings rigged before they come; a pipe is half a ton and must go into the hold gently. Ruiz goes out in the first lighter with the bill of lading for the captain to sign, and forty pounds in gold for the freight. *he takes a sealed letter from the desk and holds it out* And this, for my son in Falmouth, into the captain's own hand, please. One more thing: Ruiz tells me a Frenchman was asking questions on the quay last night. Say nothing of wine or the hour of sailing to anyone, and if you go to the tavern for Mr Hale, drink little and listen much. -> done: Senhor Bettencourt spoke ashore at Fayal

[t2167660 +602h07m] JOURNAL captain [agent.word_kept] The captain's word, kept for whoever takes the station: Back aboard, sir, with Senhor Bettencourt's letter for his son at Falmouth, now before you. His answer: two lighters from Madalena, twenty pipes each, six men and a patrão apiece, away at dusk and alongside about ten tonight; Ruiz in the first lighter with the bill of lading to sign and £40 in gold; one hooded lantern at the gangway only, the fall and slings rigged beforehand, since a pipe is half a ton; we lie where we are, out of sight of the quay. He would not take the Madeira: he wants it from your hand. Ruiz reports no schooner in the Road, the black schooner far east off Santa Maria last week, but a Frenchman in a brown coat posing as a wine buyer stood the watermen drinks last night asking what the English cutter carried and when she sailed, and went out toward the beach at Porto Pim an hour before midnight. Mr Hale, who was asked too and said nothing, is fit and his chest is corded behind the tavern bar; he did not come off in this boat, so he's to come to the quay. I advise a double lookout tonight, nobody to speak of the hour, and the boat's crew armed.

[t2168574 +602h22m] WORLD ORDER (the director): say as Mr Pascoe: Aye aye, sir. *he goes forward with Chips and comes aft again a quarter of an hour on* Carpenter's been down in the forepeak with a lantern, sir. Inside she's tight: the two strained seams by the forefoot that he stopped after the ground are holding, dry to the touch, and the well's at an inch and steady, as you saw. Outside's another thing. Looking over the bow in this clear water you can see a sheet of copper torn away on the forefoot, two foot by three, and the sheathing board under it scored where she lay on the rock. The worm will be into that bare plank by Madeira, and it slows her a little. He can't get at it afloat as she lies. If we heel her a strake or two, shifting the guns and the water to larboard and hauling down on a masthead tackle to a boat, he can nail a new sheet over it from the boat in a forenoon. He has two sheets of spare copper and the nails. Or the caulkers ashore will do it for three or four pounds, but that's more eyes on the ship, sir. -> done: Mr Pascoe spoke on the deck, heard by the officer of the watch

[t2171267 +603h07m] WORLD ORDER (the director): say as Senhor Bettencourt: *from the inner room, then the door opens* Captain! In this fog? Come in, come in. Maria, the coffee. *he sees the case under your arm and spreads his hands* So you brought it yourself after all. You shame me, Captain. Sit. Your Mr Pearce was here at dawn and carried everything exactly; a good officer, that one. The lighters are bespoke, the patrões know only that a ship in the Road wants wine, not which. And this fog is a gift from God: if it holds until night, nobody on the quay will see so much as your riding light. -> done: Senhor Bettencourt spoke ashore at Fayal
[t2171314 +603h08m] ORDER captain> give a case of the owners' Madeira to senhor bettencourt
[t2171323 +603h08m] WORLD ORDER (the director): say as Senhor Bettencourt: *he lifts out a bottle, reads the owners' mark and laughs* My own wine, gone to London and come home again to me. That is a better joke than any your owners meant. Thank you, Captain. *he opens a drawer and counts gold onto the table* And this is not for the freight; that is Ruiz's business tonight. This is for bringing my son's letter unopened across a sea with a Basque in it, and for your trouble on the rocks of my island. Ten guineas. No, I insist; it is what I would pay a packet, and you came faster than any packet. -> done: Senhor Bettencourt spoke ashore at Fayal

[t2171668 +603h14m] ORDER captain> Say to Senhor Bettencourt Indeed, mark me down for 8 pipes, and a case of bottles of the same besides for my cabin. They came ahandy once, and perhaps they shall again.
[t2171682 +603h14m] WORLD ORDER (the director): say as Senhor Bettencourt: *he writes as he speaks* Eight pipes for the captain's own account, four tons at thirty-two: one hundred and twenty-eight pounds. Pay him when the pipes are in your hold, not before; that is how we do business at Horta. *he sands the letter, folds it and calls through the door* Manuel! [t2185688 +607h08m] WORLD ORDER (the director): say as Senhor Bettencourt: *he is already reaching for his pen* Nothing easier, Captain. [t2202451 +611h47m] JOURNAL officer of the watch [agent.handover] Handover note (handing over the deck): Handover, 16:47 first dog watch, 3 July 1806. Sherbourne rides moored on two bowers (best 240 fathoms, small 120, both full out; kedge catted at the bows) in 22 fathoms; fixes each glass all day within a cable of the account (38° 32' N, 28° 37' W): Espalamaca N by E, town W, Magdalena E. Fog lifted 14:45, now clear, wind N by E 7 kn, glass 30.24 steady, moderate sea from the north. Well an inch and steady since the copper went on; you told me to avast sounding it. Variation 22° 30' W by azimuth (3 July). Water 5.5 tons, provisions 32 days. Tonight: Bettencourt's two lighters from Madalena (20 pipes each, six men and patrão each) alongside about 22:00 with Ruiz in the first, the bill of lading and £40 gold; also 8 days of provisions (£10) and two butts of fresh water free; your own 8 pipes marked C (£128 to Ruiz when stowed) and a present case of bottles; one hooded lantern at the gangway; the Frenchman in the brown coat is asking after us, so keep the hour quiet. The sail on the land breeze before dawn will need the small bower weighed, kedge catted, best bower hove short, topsail set; I'd call the larboard and starboard together for that. I have eaten and drunk and am going below to rest until called.
